entries.title: Aaron Rodgers returning for another year with Steelers
entries.summary: <p>The man who said he owns the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> isn’t going away quite yet.</p><p>Aaron Rodgers agreed Saturday night to return to the Steelers on a one-year deal. He’ll make up to $25 million, per ESPN, and give new head coach Mike McCarthy an established starter.</p><p>Rodgers was solid in his first year with the Steelers, throwing for 3,322 yards with 24 touchdowns and seven interceptions. He went 10-6 as the starter. The lone game he missed was at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/15/mayor-brandon-johnson-aide-jason-lee-chicago-bears-stadium-arlington-heights-northwest-indiana-lakefront-site" target="_blank" >Soldier Field</a>, one week after breaking a bone in his left wrist.</p><p>The Packers traded Rodgers to the Jets in April 2023, ending his 18-year stint with the Bears’ rival. He suffered a season-ending injury in his first game with the team and went 5-12 in his second season. The 42-year-old signed with the Steelers a year ago.</p><p>Despite the Steelers wanting an answer before the NFL draft, Rodgers waited to decide on a return. He was spotted eating ice cream with Steelers players Friday night and is expected to practice with the team next week.</p><p>The Bears do not play the Steelers this season.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Cubs starter Jameson Taillon tips his cap to Munetaka Murakami
entries.summary: <p>The question was directed to Cubs pitcher <b>Jameson Taillon</b>, still nursing the invisible psychic wounds left by a five-homer barrage from the White Sox in an 8-3 loss Saturday night at Rate Field.</p><p>Now that you’ve laid eyes on him, Taillon was asked, did he understand all the fuss surrounding <b>Munetaka Murakami</b>, the Japanese slugger who so far this season is outshining even the great <b>Shohei Ohtani</b>?</p><p>“Yeah, man,’’ he said of Murakami, who took Taillon deep twice, giving him 17 home runs for the season. “I can’t understand why 29 other teams weren’t interested, to be completely honest. Like some groupthink where people just decided they were out on him, and the whole league decided they were out.</p><p>“Like, it’s crazy to me. I mean, he can hit, he can put the ball in the seats, he’s young, he’s got a ton of juice, he’s got a presence up there, for sure. He controls the strike zone, he does a lot of things really well.”</p><p>Only <b>Kyle Schwarber</b>, with 20, has hit more home runs than Murakami, who had Sox owner <b>Jerry Reinsdorf</b> calling out, “Big win” to various Sox employees who waved as he made his way through the ballpark lobby.</p><p>Baseball’s beloved statistician, <b>Sarah Langs</b>, whose battle with ALS has gripped the industry, noted that Murakami and shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery</b>, who homered for the second straight night, have homered in the same game eight times this season. That’s more than any other duo in a team’s first 45 games in big-league history.</p><p>“Yeah, man, it’s crazy to me that more teams weren’t interested,’’ Taillon said. “I don’t know what the situation was, but it seems like he’s got a great fit here, and he’s comfortable here, they’ve made him feel welcome, and that’s quite a show in how he’s playing.’’</p><p><b>Swanson sits</b></p><p>Shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> was given the night off, with <b>Nico Hoerner</b> moving to short and <b>Matt Shaw</b> to second. Swanson had a double in five trips in Friday night’s 10-5 win, but in the 18 games he has played since his last home run, April 24 in Los Angeles, Swanson is batting .161, has an OPS of .422, has just three extra-base hits and four RBI. Bad luck may be playing a part: His batting average for balls in play is just .200.</p>
entries.author: Gordon Edes

entries.title: The Cubs' Alex Bregman and Pete Crow-Armstrong know they both will heat up offensively soon
entries.summary: <p>This is how close Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman have become in just a few short months.</p><p>“He’s invited me to his house a few times,’’ Crow-Armstrong said, “I’ve spent time with his kids.’’</p><p>No, he’s not yet Uncle Pete or Uncle PCA. Knox is closing in on 4, Bennett just turned 1.</p><p>“Mostly he calls me PCA or Pete-Crow Armstrong,’’ he said of the toddler. “But anytime [Bregman] wants me to babysit, I’ll do it.’’</p><p>Bregman is a 32-year-old dad from Albuquerque, a budding entrepreneur whose district attorney father, Sam Bregman, is a Democratic candidate for governor of New Mexico.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong is 24 years old, single, a Southern California kid whose parents were both in the movie and TV industry.</p><p>What has drawn them together, Bregman said, is how much the two of them talk baseball. “He’s a throwback,’’ Bregman said. “He loves the game, he works his tail off, and we have a lot of similarities in that regard. So we talk baseball all the time.’’</p><p>Crow-Armstrong is not sure he’s a throwback. “I was that way back with my boys when we were growing up,’’ he said. “But we’re both maniacs.’’</p><p>One thing they agree on: The Cubs are winning and have the second-best record in the NL, even though neither Bregman nor Crow-Armstrong have gone off yet offensively.</p><p>“He may go off any time,’’ Crow-Armstrong said. “He hit three balls [Friday night] that combined to go over 300 miles an hour.’’</p><p>The explosion, when it comes, may have to wait a bit. On Saturday night, the White Sox were acting like throwbacks themselves, Bill Veeck’s South Side Hitmen of distant memory. Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery made like Zisk, Gamble and Soderholm from a half-century ago, with four home runs and seven runs in the first five innings against Jameson Taillon. Two of the home runs were hit by the Japanese slugger, his first multi-homer game, giving him 17 for the season.</p><p>When Andrew Benintendi, who had homered just twice this season, took Taillon deep to lead off the Sox sixth, Cubs manager Craig Counsell mercifully dismissed his veteran right-hander.</p><p>But consider this: In the last 27 games entering play Saturday night, Bregman has two home runs and driven in a total of five runs, no more than one in any single game, and yet the Cubs are 21-6 in that span. What happens when Bregman starts to hit like the guy who has averaged 27 home runs and 94 RBI in a 162-game season?</p><p>“Hopefully I’ll heat up and we’ll go 21-6 again,’’ said Bregman, who beat out an infield hit and roped a double Saturday night, giving him 10 hits in his last 29 at-bats, a .345 clip.</p><p>“I don’t feel like we’ve played our best, obviously, but we’ve had different guys stepping up on different days. I think Ian [Happ] has probably shouldered a lot of the load, really, for us offensively to start this year, hitting the ball out of the ballpark, taking his walks, just putting together quality at-bat after quality at-bat. So hopefully a few more of us can get hot like that. We have a good ball club, obviously a lot of guys one through nine, and then obviously pitching and good defense. Just some complete wins, getting production from everywhere.’’</p><p>Crow-Armstrong recalls a conversation he had with Counsell when he was first summoned to the big leagues at the end of the 2023 season, in September. “He told me, I just want you here to play center field,’’ Crow-Armstrong said.</p><p>But by the All-Star break of 2025, he had morphed into more than just a pretty glove, forging the cult of PCA by putting up 25 home runs and 27 stolen bases by the All-Star break. The acrobatic center fielder? We see him on a nightly basis. That chant-inducing batsman? We haven’t seen much of him, yet, in 2026. Only occasional glimpses.</p><p>In 383 at-bats since then, not a small sample size, Crow-Armstrong is hitting .225 with 10 home runs.</p><p>“I haven’t gone off yet, either,’’ Crow-Armstrong said. “It’s been hard, it’s been very difficult, but all you can do is continue to work. Alex, he takes so many swings, it’s exhausting. He watches so much video. Me, I get in my swings, and take my game to the field. I’m going to strike out and chase, I know that. That probably won’t change until I have more experience in this game. There are still things I can take pride in. My defense, My walks. I have almost half as many walks as I had all last season. My base-running. But it is hard. You just try to work through your struggles.’’</p><p>Bregman said he tries to provide a sounding board for his struggling teammate. Is he the type to get discouraged?</p><p>“No, he works,’’ Bregman said. “He just puts his head down and works. Obviously, he knows what he’s capable of, and he just puts his head down and gets after it.’’</p><p>And what has Bregman done to try to be back to his vintage self?</p><p>“I obviously look at my swing,’’ he said, “but also game plan, basically against the pitchers I’m going to face, try and be super prepared. When I’m super prepared like that, I feel like it simplifies the game for me.’’</p><p>It will come. So says Bregman. So says Crow-Armstrong, who homered on his last at-bat, in the ninth inning. A fandom awaits.<br></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" id="rte-e8140fe0-5192-11f1-8610-fd3eab40f16d"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amq" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px 16px; vertical-align: top; width: 44px; visibility: hidden;"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amr" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px; width: 909.333px;"></td></tr></tbody></table>

entries.title: Munetaka Murakami, White Sox power past Cubs
entries.summary: <p>Before Saturday’s game against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> manager Will Venable didn’t seem too worried about Munetaka Murakami.</p><p>Venable knew what he was talking about.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/11/cubs-seiya-suzuki-counsels-white-sox-munetaka-murakami-kazuma-okamoto-shohei-ohtani" >Murakami</a> hit two of the Sox’ five home runs in their 8-3 win over the Cubs. Not only did Murakami break a six-game dry spell, he had the first multi-homer game of his MLB career and helped the Sox climb back above .500 at 23-22.</p><p>“I told you guys he’s just fine,” Venable said. “Obviously, he sets a real high expectation, continues to have good at-bats, make good swing decisions and gets really good swings off and when he does, they usually go over the fence.”</p><p>Along with Murakami, the Sox got home runs from Miguel Vargas, Colson Montgomery and Andrew Benintendi. Murakami, Vargas and Montgomery have become one of baseball’s best power trios, and they showed why Saturday.</p><p>“They are really good teammates and the centerpiece of the team, as well as everybody,” Murakami said via a translator. “I’m really happy we are on the same squad. We want to keep continuing a day like this.”</p><p>Vargas echoed that.</p><p>“We prepared for this type of moment and I think we’re doing a really good job,” Vargas said. “I feel it’s not just us three. I think it’s the whole team we’re doing a really good job in every at-bat, and I think they put us in a really good spot to drive in runs and score.”</p><p>For Murakami, hitting homers against the rival Cubs in front of a sellout crowd of 38,795 is one of his biggest Sox moments. And two months into his MLB career,<br>the ups and downs are already part of the Murakami experience.</p><p>From April 5-12, Murakami went homerless. He struck out 10 times in that period and hit .043, perhaps reminding people why his free-agent market this winter was not as robust or lucrative as expected. But not long after, Murakami hit home runs in five straight games, sparking chatter about his pace for homers in a season and a hope for power every time he stepped to the plate.</p><p>Once again, Murakami ended a rough patch with a bang, beating the Cubs’ Jameson Taillon twice.</p><p>“We’re seeing him make adjustments every day,” Venable said. “He’s learning these pitchers for the first time, this is his first time seeing all these guys. He’s able to make [adjustments] in games, pitch-to-pitch,<br>at-bat to at-bat.”</p><p>Murakami was expected to be a “three true outcomes” hitter, one who either hits a home run, strikes out or walks often. That has not been wrong — entering Saturday, Murakami had 15 home runs, one behind the Yankees’ Aaron Judge for the American League lead. His 35 walks were fourth in the AL, and his 64 strikeouts were the most in the American League.</p><p>Regardless of the strikeouts, Murakami has made an impression on his teammates.</p><p>“He’s a superstar. There’s no other way to [put] it,” said Sox starter Davis Martin, who went six innings and allowed one run. “You play against guys like [Mike] Trout, you play against guys like Judge and Yordan Alvarez and he’s doing the same things that they are. It’s an incredible thing to watch.”</p><p>Murakami has been a spark for a franchise that desperately needed one, exciting fans and pushing teammates.</p><p>And he’s actually exciting to his teammates as well.</p><p>“From a starting pitcher’s perspective, you have four nights where you’re not throwing, where you have front-row seats and you’re expecting him to do something crazy,” Martin said.<br></p>

entries.title: Blackhawks need to be aggressive with trade offers if any NHL stars hit market this summer
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> general manager Kyle Davidson continues to express more eagerness to make trades. </p><p>If a high-end player becomes available, Davidson has asserted he will <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/03/14/blackhawks-nhl-trade-possibilities-robert-thomas-jason-robertson-matthew-knies" target="_blank" >try to acquire him</a>.</p><p>Over the next several months, that stance will be put to the test. If no high-end players move around the NHL this summer, it will be simply unfortunate for the Hawks, not reprehensible.</p><p>But if any high-end players do move, the Hawks need to do absolutely everything within their power to ensure they're the team to which that player moves.</p><p>Davidson has consistently followed through on his words so far in his GM tenure, to his credit. He declared he would undergo a lengthy rebuild, accumulating as many high draft picks as possible and building through youth without rushing the process, and there's no question he has done exactly that, whether or not fans like it.</p><p>Now it's time for him to not only follow through on his words once again but also swing for fences beyond the relatively low expectations he has set.</p><p>"We are always trying to explore options to improve, and we have, and it hasn't occurred," Davidson said April 16. "I think we're far more active in our attempts than people may think, but...it has to make sense, and it can't compromise the makeup of our group — or the core of our group — that we've got here.</p><p>"We're definitely going to explore what's out there. I don't think I'm shy to try things. Just nothing has arisen in the last little while to make that happen. But we're going to look at what we can do to add to the roster, of course. We've got a lot of assets, should we find something that is available to us that we want in the trade market."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Davidson has repeatedly blamed lack of availability for the lack of activity. He's correct that the past few summers have been less fruitful, due to the skyrocketing NHL salary cap giving teams almost unlimited flexibility to re-sign important players before they reach market.</p><p>In terms of the total quantity of notable available players, this coming summer seems equally bleak. Sabres forward Alex Tuch and Ducks defenseman John Carlson are two of relatively few notable free agents who should interest the Hawks.</p><p>But there are a number of team-specific scenarios that could, if they play out, seriously shake the league.</p><p>What if Stars GM Jim Nill determines he doesn't have enough cap space to re-sign restricted free-agent Jason Robertson? Or what if the Stars' dearth of five-on-five goals during their first-round loss to the Wild convinces Nill he can't win a Stanley Cup with this current core?</p><p>What if new Blues GM Alexander Steen shares exiting GM Doug Armstrong's belief that the Blues need to retool? Armstrong already dangled Robert Thomas at the deadline, and Jordan Kyrou could also join that conversation.</p><p>What if Senators GM Steve Staios responds dramatically to captain Brady Tkachuk's tumultuous season and poor playoff performance and listens to offers on him? Staios shut down that topic during Senators exit interviews, but Tkachuk called the increasing trade rumors a legitimate "distraction."</p><p>What if Jets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff, after listening to centerpiece goalie Connor Hellebuyck's despondent exit interview, decide to shake up the league's most disappointing team from this past season?</p><p>How will leadership changes within the Maple Leafs, Devils, Kraken, Canucks and Predators affect those franchises' directions? The Rangers and Penguins, despite very different results this season, also fall in the same bucket as the Predators as teams with aging rosters staring down difficult decisions.</p><p>This is the most unstable the league has been in a few years, although that's largely because the past few years have been remarkably stagnant in terms of the league hierarchy. The young Canadiens, Ducks, Flyers and Sharks' rises this year indicate that stagnation is loosening.</p><p>One big question is what controversial new Leafs GM John Chayka will do, particularly after receiving the gift of winning the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/05/05/blackhawks-draft-pick-nhl-lottery-gavin-mckenna-ivar-stenberg-kyle-davidson" target="_blank" >draft lottery</a>. </p><p>Can he earn the reportedly shaky trust of superstar Auston Matthews? Will he follow in predecessor Brad Treliving's steps and resume shopping young power forward Matthew Knies?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-credit"><p>Sean Kilpatrick/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Davidson owes it to Hawks fans to inquire about any and all difference-making players who come within a mile of the trade market. The Hawks need to try to join the Canadiens-Ducks-Flyers-Sharks group next season.</p><p>No stone should be left unturned — not with the enormous pool of assets the Hawks have to offer, a pool which should now include this year's No. 4 overall pick.</p><p>And difference-making forwards shouldn't be the only stones turned over, either. The Hawks learned down the stretch this season that a defense composed entirely of players under age 25 might not be a recipe for success.</p><p>"There's people that I have to get to know and get to understand what direction they're going with their clubs, but that's a pretty quick process," Davidson said May 5.</p><p>"Based on a lot of the press conferences by both new and sitting managers, it feels like everyone's looking to add. Those are interesting waters to navigate when everyone's trying to do the same thing."</p><p>That's true, and that's one of several reasons why there's a looming sense of dread — despite all of this potential chaos — that actually very few opportunities will arise for the Hawks to make a splash. </p><p>Even the Knies possibility, which always seemed most realistic and doable, feels less so now after the Leafs' lottery win. It would've been more logical for them to deal him — and they would've been more attracted to the No. 4 pick — had they lost their protected first-round pick to the Bruins.</p><p>The Robertson possibility, on the other hand, might be gaining steam, since the Stars are reportedly reluctant to pay him more than Mikko Rantanen's $12 million cap hit. But would Nill even entertain trading Robertson within the Central Division?</p><p>Enough time has passed that the Hawks can now dangle young NHL players like Oliver Moore, Ryan Greene, Nick Lardis and Sam Rinzel in negotiations, rather than solely picks and prospects. That could make their offers more enticing to teams not willing to entertain full-scale rebuilds, which it seems no teams currently are.</p><p>And it's worth noting the rest of the league's stubborn refusal to rebuild, if it holds, should eventually benefit the Hawks, since the age curve eventually comes for everyone. Nobody else is even attempting to build a young core that could rival the Hawks' or Sharks' come, say, 2030.</p><p>But that stubbornness could also inhibit the Hawks' chances to jumpstart or accelerate their ascension past its natural speed right now in 2026. </p><p>Only time will tell how many chances do arise and how realistic they are. The Hawks can't let any slip by them.</p><p><b>NOTE: </b>The Hawks officially signed Russian prospect <b>Roman Kantserov</b> to a three-year NHL entry-level contract Thursday. It carries a $1.075 million salary-cap hit.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Brother batters sibling with stinging insults
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My brother has found love again. His first wife passed away from cancer two years ago. He is getting married in two months. We were never super close but have always been civil to each other and spent an hour or two with each other during holiday meals or birthdays.</p><p>Our mother is 89 and lives at his home in an added-on apartment. She's our common denominator. Because my brother is quick-tempered and short with me (and others), I'm afraid that after Mom is gone, he will have no use for me and I'll never see him again.</p><p>I sent him an email stating my fear, and his reply was shocking. He said he didn't like my facial expressions. He also said he doesn't like my mannerisms and feels nothing I say is genuine, but very fake. He also told me he wasn't alone in those thoughts. I felt like he had stuck a knife through my heart. He said he wished he had a video of me so I could see how fake I was. I cried and got physically ill.</p><p>I am so embarrassed that he and others see me that way that I have decided not to go to his wedding. I cannot be in a room full of people who have made these judgments about my integrity. Am I making the right choice? Should I go for my mother's sake? — <i>STUNNED AND EMBARRASSED</i></p><p><b>DEAR STUNNED:</b> Your brother may have found love again, but he has some real problems. That he would speak to you that way was cruel and deliberately hurtful. Could he have some unresolved sibling rivalry? If that's the case, you cannot fix it for him.</p><p>Under the circumstances, not wanting to attend that wedding is understandable. However, just because your brother says something does not make it true. They may be his feelings, but he doesn't have the right to speak for all your other relatives. That is why I hope you will maintain your relationships with the rest of the family and not allow him to drive you away.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mother comes over to visit every single evening at 7:30. She knows that I must be up early and leave the house at 5:30 a.m. to go to work. I have dropped numerous hints, but she's oblivious. This causes a lot of stress in my marriage. My partner thinks it's ridiculous to visit someone at 7:30 every night, especially since I have two kids who need rides home from practices in the evenings. Please help. — <i>AT WITS' END</i></p><p><b>DEAR WITS' END:</b> Because you have already tried talking to your mother about this but she doesn't get the message, enlist the help of your partner and talk to her together. When you do, establish a realistic schedule for her visits — two days a week, perhaps — and how long they will last. Then, when the time is up, escort her to the door.</p><p>Your mother may do this because she has no life of her own. If that's a contributing factor, start researching groups of seniors she might join for activities other than visiting her daughter every night. If you do, it may vastly improve the quality of her life and the lives of those in your household.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For everything you need to know about wedding planning, order "How to Have a Lovely Wedding." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby, Wedding Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

</div> </div><p></p><h4>Is flooding getting worse?</h4><p>Big thunderstorms are becoming more frequent and dropping more rain in a short period of time. The streets and local sewers across Chicago and the Cook County suburbs are not designed to handle so much rain, and that’s sending water into streets and homes.</p><p>Basement flooding is chronic and widespread, especially in low-income communities of color, where streets and outdated sewer infrastructure have seen few improvements and green space is lacking.</p><p>Severe storms causing flooding, hail and tornadoes resulted in losses of $50 billion across the U.S. in each of the past three years, according to the industry research group Insurance Information Institute.</p><h4>How do I know if I need flood insurance?</h4><p>Almost every community in the Chicago area is at risk of flooding. Neighborhood sewers are designed to hold 2 inches of rain in a 24-hour period. Some storms are dumping four times that amount. The same goes for suburban Cook County.</p><p>The rain is landing so hard and so fast that it overwhelms the sewers and doesn’t allow the water to run through a massive flood-mitigation system known as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/5/10/18451028/thornton-quarry-the-grand-canyon-of-the-south-suburbs-will-soon-be-underwater" >Deep Tunnel</a>.</p><p>Many homeowners are finding out that they don’t have the right insurance to cover losses from water in their homes.</p><h4>How do I figure out if my existing homeowner’s insurance covers basement flooding? </h4><p>Major insurers, such as State Farm and Allstate, will not automatically cover sewer-backup basement flooding as part of a regular homeowner’s plan.</p><p>Since 1968, the federal government has been the primary insurer for flooding across the country.</p><p>Allstate says it bluntly on its website: “No type of flood damage, no matter the source of the water, is covered by standard homeowners policies.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-350000" name="image-350000"></a> <picture It didn’t.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Giacomo Cain/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Larry Quinn Jr., who lives in Austin, thought his State Farm homeowners insurance would cover flooding. In 2023, more than five feet of water flooded his basement through the sewer drains.</p><p>“The water was shooting up through the sewers. I mean literally shooting up,” Quinn says.</p><p>Water ruined two furnaces, several appliances, large power tools, an electric circuit board and so far has cost Quinn about $70,000 in total damages. His insurance didn’t cover the costs to repair or replace anything, he says.</p><p>State Farm says it encourages people to review their policies with their agents.</p><p>Here’s what to look for in your policy: Your homeowner’s insurance will list a number of “exclusions,” including damage from water. You need to ask your agent about additional coverage, often referred to as an “endorsement” that will cover basement sewer backup that damages personal items as well as structural things, such as a furnace.</p><p>It’s important to run through multiple scenarios with an insurer or agent to make sure you’re buying the right kind of coverage.</p><p>For example: Ask “am I covered in the case of sewer water backing up into my basement?”</p><h4>If my insurer won’t issue flood insurance to me or doesn’t offer it, what options do I have? </h4><p>Add-on insurance from private companies can be at least several hundred dollars but risk will be a big determinant whether you can even buy the coverage. Make sure you understand what a policy pays for either structural damage or for personal property.</p><p>The government offers flood insurance plans for people in flood-prone areas through the National Flood Insurance Program. But the federal government plan, available to everyone in Chicago and much of Cook County, can have limited coverage of basement damage. It won’t cover personal items stored in a basement or any remodeling done to a finished area.</p><p>Federal flood insurance can cost at least $700 a year. Estimated quotes can be calculated at <a class="Link" href="https://www.floodsmart.gov" target="_blank" ><u>https://www.floodsmart.gov</u></a>. entries.title: As Red Line expands, South and West Siders run along 103rd Street to imagine something new
entries.summary: <p>More than 360 Chicagoans from the West and South sides ran three miles along 103rd Street to exercise and reimagine what the corridor could become.</p><p>Runners gathered at Corliss Early College STEM High School in Pullman for the inaugural 103rd Street 5K Peace Walk/Run. The event ended at Percy L. Julian High School with a vendor fair and community conversation about how vacant lots could be transformed into businesses and community centers.</p><p>In April, the Chicago Transit Authority <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/04/24/red-line-extension-cta-groundbreaking-federal-funding-freeze-trump-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>broke ground on the Red Line Extension Project</u></a>, which includes a station planned for 103rd Street. Community organizations are now working to revitalize the corridor from Cottage Grove Avenue to Vincennes Avenue in anticipation of increased traffic and investment in the neighborhood.</p><p>In an effort to bridge communities across the city, West Side runners from Peace Runners 773 run club joined South Side residents to imagine new possibilities for the 103rd Street corridor — from restaurants and gyms to community centers.</p><p>“I didn't run past one grocery store within three miles, and it's the same thing on the West Side,” said Jackie Hoffman, founder and executive director of the Peace Runners.</p><p>Hoffman started the run club <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/12/17/west-garfield-park-death-gap-life-expectancy-racial-cancer-heart-disease-racial" target="_blank" ><u>to address Chicago’s death gap</u></a> on the West Side.</p><p>“It's a lot of West Siders that have never been to the South Side until today, and a lot of South Siders that will be coming to the West Side, " Hoffman said. “As we keep uniting throughout the city, we create these really big movements that reclaim our spaces, and get the things that we need for our communities.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div visible disinvestment between two affluent neighborhoods, Beverly to the west and Pullman to the east,” Strandberry said. “This corridor can use a little bit more love.”</p><p>Organizers welcomed representatives from the Chicago Transit Authority to get direct feedback from community members about the project.</p><p>Tammy Chase, a spokesperson for the Red Line Extension Project, said the city is trying to correct decades of inequitable transit access that contributed to longer commutes for South Side residents.</p><p>“We keep hearing from constituents who want grocery stores, and they want class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Shequira Hall noticed the vacant lots and abandoned buildings while running the inaugural 103rd 5K. Hall said the community support she received throughout the run inspired her to join more run club events in the future.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Somer Van Benton/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Shequira Hall has lived in neighborhoods on both the South and West sides of Chicago. Though she doesn’t consider herself a runner, she said participants helped pace and encourage her through the 5K.</p><p>“There were people who were out here handing us waters and Gatorades, and people were driving down the street, honking their horns, and very supportive,” she said. “But I do feel like we need more businesses on the South Side, and down 103rd street, in particular.”</p><p>Pullman resident Mary Zehnder was born and raised on Chicago’s South Side.</p><p>“I was surprised at how much support was along the way,” Zehnder said. “We're going down the street and people are honking their horns and waving. That's how communities become really alive.”</p><p>West Side resident Therese Franklin said she had only ever driven along 103rd Street before the race. Running the corridor drew her attention to beauty shops and neighborhood stores along the route.</p><p>“There are a lot of small businesses that need community support to stay in business,” Franklin said. “Getting out here and seeing them makes me want to come back and actually support those businesses.”</p><p>The event was supported by organizations including Chicago’s Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events and the Roosmoor Community Association. Public officials, including State Rep. Justin Slaughter and Democratic nominee Shantel Franklin, also attended.</p><p>Participants ranged in age from toddlers in strollers to older adults, leaving the event with gold medals to celebrate both their run and their commitment to the community.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally shot in West Englewood, police say
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot and killed in West Englewood Saturday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 37, was in the 5700 block of South Damen Avenue around 10:40 p.m. when someone fired shots, striking him in the arm and buttocks, police said in a statement.</p><p>He was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center and pronounced dead, police said. No arrests were reported.</p>

entries.title: Review: Bruno Mars shows why he’s everyone’s favorite showman at sold-out Chicago concert
entries.summary: <p>Before Bruno Mars took the stage for The Romantic Tour’s sold-out Soldier Field show on Saturday, Anderson .Paak performed a DJ set organized by decade.</p><p>Disguised as DJ Pee.Wee — silky bob wig and all — the artist, who is touring with Mars, played hits by ABBA and Whitney Houston for the ’70s and ’80s babies. Then, he spun “Macarena,” “Teach Me How to Dougie” and Travis Scott’s “Fein” for those born in the ’90s, early aughts and beyond. (Chicago trumpeter Maurice MOBETTA Brown provided accompaniment.)</p><p>The enthusiastic reception of each song underscored Mars’ ability to attract a multigenerational audience. People of all ages not only showed up but dressed up, donning red outfits to match the visual aesthetic of the crooner’s latest record, “The Romantic.” Women adorned their hair with roses, men tied bandannas around their heads and some even wore silk pajamas resembling his “24K Magic” album cover.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Ramos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>.Paak returned to the stage to join Mars for a few songs from their collaborative album, “An Evening with Silk Sonic.” The two delighted with some lovely harmonies and a playful vocal battle, which they called a “yearn-off,” during “Leave the Door Open.” But one of the night’s best moments happened when Mars couldn’t contain his laughter while singing a silly line from “Smokin out the Window”: “Got her bad — kids runnin’ ’round my whole crib like it's Chuck E. Cheese.”</p><p>It was a rare moment of breaking character for Mars. If any criticism is to be levied against him, it might be that his shows are, at times, <i>too</i> polished. For example, the ballad “Why You Wanna Fight?” — a highlight of “The Romantic” — could have benefited from a rawer performance; though his singing was top-tier, the number, which included a dramatic drop to one knee, seemed more choreographed than organic. The lyrics of the song, like others on his latest album, don’t read as a peek into Mars’ real-life loves and heartbreaks. Even after all of his time in the industry, there’s still some mystery about the person behind the performer. “The Romantic” is his first solo effort in nearly a decade. What has happened in his life during that time, and might he ever tap into that on a record?</p><p>For now, his fans are still keen to celebrate the past. During the second set, the crowd sang every line of his older pop hits, including “Marry You,” “Locked Out of Heaven” and “Just the Way You Are.” During a superb acoustic piano set, all he had to do was hit the first chord of “When I Was Your Man” to elicit screams. He closed with “Uptown Funk” and “Dance With Me,” remarkably ending a night with vocals as strong as when it began. <b></b> And he’ll do it all again at another sold-out show at Soldier Field on Sunday. <b></b></p><p>“Chicago, I love you forever,” he said. “Could I stay with you forever?”</p><p>At this point, who is going to say no?<b> </b></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Man fatally shot during argument in South Shore home
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot and killed during an argument in a South Shore home Sunday morning, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man, 28, was arguing with someone at a residence in the 2700 block of East 75th Street at 9:40 a.m. when they pulled a gun and fired shots, striking him in the chest, police said in a statement.</p><p>The man was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, police said. His identity has not been released.</p><p>The suspect fled the scene, police said. No one was in custody.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Gage Park woman charged with fatally stabbing infant daughter during argument with father
entries.summary: <p>A woman has been charged with fatally stabbing her infant daughter in Gage Park after allegedly arguing with the child's father about waking up her other children.</p><p>Tatiana Maxwell, 25, faces murder charges in connection to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/15/infant-girl-fatally-stabbed-in-gage-park-on-southwest-side-one-held" target="_blank" >the Friday morning incident</a> that left her less than one-month-old daughter, Nyhnia Stovall, dead, Chicago police announced Sunday.</p><p>Maxwell was allegedly arguing with Nyhnia's father about waking up her other two sons when he ran out of their apartment in the 3000 block of West 59th Street, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>According to the report, which quoted the father, the dad allegedly told a neighbor that Maxwell was going through postpartum depression and was "going to kill the newborn." </p><p>The neighbor later told police that the father said the mother had been listening to "satanic music," according to the report.</p><p>Nyhnia's dad tried to go back inside but the door was locked, according to the report. He kicked the door in and found Maxwell lying on the floor next to Nyhnia, who had a stab wound to her chest, according to the report.</p><p>When police and ambulances showed up, Maxwell allegedly jumped from a second-story window, injuring herself, police said.</p><p>She was taken into police custody and treated at the University of Chicago Medical Center, and the child was pronounced dead at Comer Children’s Hospital, according to police. The Illinois Department of Children and Family Services was notified, the police report said.</p>
entries.author: Mary Norkol

entries.title: New knee issue adds to intrigue surrounding White Sox catcher Kyle Teel
entries.summary: <p>The wait for Kyle Teel might have been extended.</p><p>Playing for Triple-A Charlotte on Saturday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/10/white-sox-catcher-kyle-teel-rehab-assignment-tuesday-charlotte-munetaka-murakami-cal-raleigh" >during his long-awaited rehab stint</a>, Teel tweaked his right knee during a swing. Teel was not in Charlotte’s lineup Sunday, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> manager Will Venable said the 24-year-old catcher will be reevaluated Monday.</p><p>On March 10, Teel strained his right hamstring playing for Team Italy in the World Baseball Classic. He finally began his rehab assignment Tuesday, raising hope that his return would be imminent.</p><p>Venable didn’t seem too alarmed by the Teel situation.</p><p>“It would be premature to get too down the road on where we’re at or evaluate the concern for it,” Venable said. “We just want to figure out what is going on there and evaluate where’s he’s at, see how he responded to the treatment from last night and go from there.”</p><p>Without Teel, the Sox have used Edgar Quero, Drew Romo and Reese McGuire behind the plate. The results haven’t been great: Sox catchers have combined to hit .166 with a .271 on-base percentage.</p><p>At least recently, Romo has given the Sox something from the position. He has four homers and a .364 on-base percentage. The pitchers also seem to like throwing to him. Davis Martin said Saturday that Romo can correct him when a pitch misses and picks up a batter’s movement in the box.</p><p>“Drew brings in what he saw the day before and a really good picture of what their offense is trying to do to us and how fast we can make those adjustments,” said Martin, who has an 0.96 ERA over 18 2/3 innings throwing to Romo. “He’s a calming presence back there and he’s been incredible.”</p>
entries.author: Brian Sandalow

entries.title: Umpire Brian O'Nora out indefinitely after sustaining concussion during Cubs-White Sox game Saturday night
entries.summary: <p>Brian O’Nora, who has been umpiring in the major leagues since 1992, will be out indefinitely after he said he sustained a concussion during the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> game Saturday night in Rate Field.</p><p>O’Nora was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/16/versatile-sean-newcomb-a-valuable-piece-of-white-sox-bullpen" >struck in the left side of the jaw</a> by a foul ball off the bat of Jarred Kelenic in the fourth inning of Saturday’s 8-3 White Sox win. The force of the blow dropped him to a knee.</p><p>“I’ve been doing this for [34] years,’’ O’Nora said Sunday morning, “and that’s the best shot I’ve taken in the face.</p><p>“I don’t remember anything until I got up. I have bad headaches and the left side of my jaw is very sore.’’</p><p>O’Nora, after being looked at by Sox trainers, was removed from the game, with Erich Bacchus taking his place behind the plate and the umpires finishing the game with a three-man crew.</p><p>Triple-A umpire John Bacon, a designated call-up umpire, joined the crew for Sunday afternoon’s game.</p><p>O’Nora, who was in the umpires’ dressing room before the game Sunday morning, said he planned to go home later that day then to fly to Arizona to be treated at the Sports Concussion Center at Banner-University Phoenix.</p><p>“There will be all kinds of testing,’’ O’Nora said. “They won’t let me go back on the field until I get cleared.’’</p>
entries.author: Gordon Edes

entries.title: U. of C. faculty and parents protest Lab School policy they say limits classroom discussion, inclusion
entries.summary: <p>Students, parents and teachers at a private school run by the University of Chicago are rallying against a policy they say limits what students are exposed to at school and hurts teachers’ ability to support marginalized students.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1775123874/chicagolab/eajqxbdbjw5x84yvf6vw/StandardsforViewpoint-NeutralEducationinSupportofStudent-CenteredOpenInquiry.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>A new policy</u></a> at the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools, which serve around 2,000 students from preschool through high school, establishes “standards for viewpoint-neutral education” and gives teachers guidance on how to handle “contested issues.”</p><p>School administrators say the policy, which had gotten pushback since a draft was first shared in January, is meant to encourage students to become “independent thinkers” and support “open inquiry.”</p><p>“The purpose of viewpoint-neutral education is not to limit inquiry or discourage engagement with difficult, important, or contested topics,” the policy states. “Rather, the goal is to ensure that Lab classrooms and school spaces remain… places where students can encounter, explore, and evaluate important questions without being steered toward or away from particular conclusions by the authority of adults.”</p><p>But dozens of parents, many of whom are faculty at the University of Chicago, say the policy actually restricts conversations in the classroom and could prevent teachers from creating an inclusive environment for students.</p><p>Some faculty members, led by the university’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors, gathered on the school’s Hyde Park campus Friday to <a class="Link" href="https://www.uchicagoaaup.org/statements/lab-school-viewpoint-neutrality" target="_blank" ><u>deliver a petition to administrators opposing the policy</u></a>. Many wore shirts that read “free teachers raise thinkers” and held signs with the phrase “Love is love, neutrality enables hate, let our teachers advocate.”</p><p>“Usually rules that restrict what people can say are called censorship,” Patrick Morrissey, a professor of poetry at U. of C., said at the protest.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dozens of Lab School parents and students and University of Chicago faculty gathered at the university on Friday to celebrate “the diversity of thought and experience” at the Lab Schools and to protest a policy they say is an “attempt to stifle” that.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ethan Bueno de Mesquita, interim director of the Lab Schools and dean of the Harris School of Public Policy, said the policy allows students to form their own opinions.</p><p>"The standards do not avoid contested issues, but create the conditions where students learn to question assumptions, examine and debate competing arguments respectfully, and arrive at their own conclusions about such issues," Bueno de Mesquita said in a statement.</p><p>The new policy has attracted attention because the Lab Schools are known for their academic rigor and experiential learning and some worry the policy will undermine that approach.</p><p>Other parents support the policy, saying that teacher advocacy had begun to overshadow academics in the classroom, according to reporting in the University of Chicago’s student newspaper, <a class="Link" href="https://chicagomaroon.com/52330/grey-city/uchicagos-lab-school-is-split-over-new-viewpoint-neutral-education-policy/" target="_blank" ><u>the Chicago Maroon</u></a>. Some parents said the policy encourages multiple viewpoints on current events and sticky real-world issues.</p><p>“If you care about diversity, you should be delighted that there’s an emphasis now on diversity of viewpoints,” a parent who declined to be named told the Maroon.</p><p>The policy says teachers are allowed to take a stance on “widely settled historical judgments,” like denouncing slavery and the Holocaust, but taking a position on current debates is discouraged.</p><p>A “frequently asked questions” document related to the policy identifies several “active areas of disagreement in contemporary public debate” where teachers should remain neutral, including abortion, immigration laws and enforcement, policing and climate policy.</p><p>The policy says Lab School classrooms will still be welcoming to all students, but protesters worry some students’ identities and beliefs are tied up with ongoing political debates, and that could make them feel ostracized.</p><p>For example, some worry the policy is especially difficult for transgender students, as the Trump administration continues to put forward policies that target trans people. Federal officials are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lgbtq/2025/03/25/whats-at-stake-when-feds-investigate-local-accommodations-for-trans-students" target="_blank" ><u>investigating Chicago Public Schools</u></a> for allowing trans students to use the bathroom that aligns with their gender identity and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/04/30/noble-charter-network-suburban-school-districts-face-federal-probe-over-lgbtq-related-lessons" target="_blank" ><u>other schools in Illinois</u></a> over whether parents are allowed to opt out of lessons that talk about gender identity.</p><p>“Let’s be clear that neutrality that refuses to protect vulnerable children is not neutrality at all,” said Michele Friedner, a U. of C. professor who has a transgender child at one of the Lab Schools and felt like her child was already separated from other students when they were made to room with the only other trans students on a school field trip.</p><p>“Think about what this means for a child, for children, to walk into a school and understand that the institution is debating whether you deserve recognition, protection, or dignity at all,” Friedner said.</p><p>The debate at the Lab Schools takes place against the backdrop of the Trump administration’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/03/14/g-s1-53831/dei-universities-education-department-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion</u></a> in K-12 and higher education and efforts to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2025/07/01/trump-threatens-sex-ed-funding-over-gender-identity-and-trans-youth/" target="_blank" ><u>remove instruction about LGBTQ people</u></a> and themes from school lessons. Some see this policy as similarly controlling classroom conversations.</p><p>“Let’s be clear, that’s what contested issues are: Anything that might upset the Trump administration, its collaborators, and those who wish to curry favor with him,” Morrissey said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>University of Chicago professor Jessica Darrow (center) said her seventh grader has seen how the new policy can limit classroom conversations and prevent teachers from taking a stance on issues, such as whether students should try to put a stop to bullying if they see it happen.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And while the U. of C. takes a similar approach by not taking stands as a university on certain political and social issues, faculty members raised concerns that a similar policy could be adopted that would more directly affect how they teach. Jessica Darrow, a professor in the university’s Crown School of Social Work, said social justice is central to her work and a neutrality policy could go against her profession’s code of ethics.</p><p>“My students need to be able to learn to take a stand on social issues and not remain value-neutral on issues,” Darrow said.</p><p>Darrow has two sons who’ve attended the Lab Schools. She commended several parts of how the schools work, including their focus on experiential and play-based learning.</p><p>But she thinks administrators are overstepping with this policy.</p><p>Darrow’s younger son is in seventh grade at a Lab School, and he also takes issue with the policy, she said. He appreciates hearing his teachers’ thoughts and feelings during lessons, and he learns more about how to interact with others when his teachers aren’t worried about violating the policy.</p><p>Darrow said her seventh grader saw the policy’s negative effects during a recent classroom conversation about bullying. His teacher explained the difference between a “bystander,” someone who merely observes bullying or other harmful behavior, and an “upstander,” someone who tries to put a stop to it. Darrow’s son told her the teacher stopped short of recommending which path students should take because he didn’t want to be reprimanded for violating the policy.</p><p>“I think that’s where the problem lies,” Darrow said. “The chilling effect of these standards on our teachers’ ability to really do their jobs well.”</p>

entries.title: Body pulled from Lake Michigan near Oak Street Beach
entries.summary: <p>The body of a man was pulled from Lake Michigan near Oak Street Beach on the Near North Side on Friday, police said.</p><p>The man, whose age and identity were unknown, was recovered from the lake in the 1000 block of North DuSable Lake Shore Drive just before 4 p.m., police said in a statement.</p><p>Detectives will conduct a death investigation pending autopsy results from the Cook County Medical Examiner's Office, police said.</p>

entries.title: Courtney Vandersloot is 'getting really close' to returning to play
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — There's still no timeline on <b>Courtney Vandersloot's</b> return. But progress for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> point guard is apparent.</p><p>At shootaround Sunday, Vandersloot ran through the team's sets, looking indistinguishable from the active players. Afterward she stayed to play one-on-one against a player development coach.</p><p>"She's getting really close," head coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> said. "She's been working her way back progressively within the last few weeks from more of an on-court standpoint and contact standpoint."</p><p>Vandersloot, 37, tore her ACL on June 7 of last season. Players typically take 9 to 12 months to recover, and she's approaching the 12-month mark. At media day April 30, she said she feels like she's entered a more mental phase of recovery.</p><p>"So much of it was physical early on, and now we're getting to the point where the brain has to catch up with all the work," Vandersloot said. "I finally feel like a basketball player again."</p><p>Feedback on her play from teammates and coaches has been excellent. Rookie Aicha Coulibaly, who just returned from an ACL injury of her own, is impressed.</p><p>"She looks amazing," Coulibaly told the Sun-Times. "Being somebody that went through the same thing from injuries, I know she's gonna come and elevate this team."</p><p>Marsh says the team looks instantly different when Vandersloot is able to step in — and expects a major impact this season.</p><p>"She's got a chip on her shoulder to come back and feels like she has some things to prove," he said.</p><p>Once she's back, the Sky will have three seasoned ballhandlers in Vandersloot, Skylar Diggins and Natasha Cloud. How Marsh manages that backcourt rotation isn't entirely clear. Diggins has expressed a desire to play more off the ball, and Marsh has talked about using Cloud as a "utility player” capable of playing anywhere.</p><p><b>Same boat for Sevens</b></p><p><b>Azurá Stevens</b> is in a similar position as Vandersloot: still no exact return timeline, but making progress.</p><p>Marsh had hoped Stevens might be available for the road trip that ended in Minnesota, Stevens is once again ruled out against the Lynx.</p><p>"We're not in a rush," Marsh said on Friday. "We want her to be as healthy as possible. We want to take as much pressure off her to feel like she's got to rush her rehab process to get back before she's fully ready."</p><p>Stevens is recovering from a minor stress injury in her left knee. Sky leading scorer <b>Rickea Jackson</b> is beginning to anticipate her return.</p><p>"We were just texting about it," Jackson said. "Like, I can't wait to have you out here to space the floor, have her out there shooting threes and just be who she is. Definitely miss her out there."</p><p><b>Skylar Diggins questionable</b></p><p>Diggins was being evaluated during shootaround and is listed as questionable with an eye injury. She took a hit to the face in the second quarter of Friday's game against the Mercury. Marsh said he believed the foul should have been upgraded to a flagrant.</p>

entries.title: Believe in the White Sox? Their confidence is growing and rightly so after Sunday's 9-8 win over the Cubs
entries.summary: <p>Catcher Edgar Quero recalled saying during spring training that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> have a really good team. It sounded nice but maybe not realistic: the Sox had lost at least 100 games in three straight seasons, and seemed years away from being decent, let alone really good.</p><p>Maybe Quero knew something before the rest of the baseball world. Or maybe Quero and the Sox were faking it until they made it real.</p><p>Well, almost two months into the season, the Sox look real.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/edgar-quero-white-sox-rally-past-cubs-to-take-crosstown-series" >Quero’s two-run walk-off home run</a> in the 10th inning Sunday gave the Sox a 9-8 win over the Cubs. In front of a rowdy and split crowd of 38,608, the Sox finished off a 7-2 homestand, their best of at least nine games since an 8-2 run in late June and early July 2008.</p><p>“It means a lot for everybody in the clubhouse,” Quero said. “It means a lot to win this series. It means a lot for everybody, especially since we are playing really good baseball. I’m happy for this team.”</p><p>The Sox haven’t had much to be happy about for years. They’re a franchise in the middle of their second massive rebuild in a decade, and little was expected of them in 2026 other than some progress.</p><p>But this homestand that ended showed they might be ahead of schedule. Over the nine games, they proved they can win a variety of ways. There was the tense 2-1 win last Sunday over the Mariners, the sweep of the Royals when they scored six runs in each game and Saturday night’s power display when they hit five home runs.</p><p>Then there was the resilience they showed Sunday, when they trailed 3-0 and 4-1.</p><p>“They’ve just continued to play all nine innings, every single pitch,” manager Will Venable said.</p><p>That the homestand ended with a series win over the rival Cubs – their first since 2022 – just gives the Sox more momentum before they head west to play the Mariners and Giants.</p><p>“Obviously the rivalry is a big thing,” said Tristan Peters, whose three-run eighth-inning home run gave the Sox a 7-4 lead. “We know that they're a good team, but we also believe that we're a really good team too. And we just proved that.”</p><p>This Sox team is clearly not perfect. If they’re going to actually contend in the American League, they’ll need to help the bullpen, a sore spot that hurt them Sunday when Seranthony Dominguez gave up Michael Conforto’s game-tying three-run homer in the ninth. Despite Davis Martin’s emergence, the rotation could use at least another proven arm. And there’s no proof the Sox lineup can keep producing the way it has over a full 162-game season, maybe under the pressure of a playoff race when each at-bat gets more intense.</p><p>Yet as this homestand and Sunday highlighted, these Sox have earned some trust. And even if they don’t make a run, things feel much better than they have recently, like it’s a franchise that’s actually going the right way after years of burning goodwill with their fans.</p><p>The victories also feel legit. This version of the Sox doesn’t have to tell themselves they’re capable of winning or convince rightfully skeptical outsiders.</p><p>“We're bringing in the right guys, we're bringing in great leadership with our coaching staff, we're bringing in great teammates,” shortstop Colson Montgomery said. “The whole ‘fake it till you make it’ thing, it can be true and it can be contagious. Once you start winning, it's like all right, this is real, it's not fake. I think what we have going on here is real.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs' Jameson Taillon searching for fixes after another homer-heavy outing
entries.summary: <p>There’s a reason you don’t often see pitchers give up five home runs in a game, like the Cubs’ <b>Jameson Taillon</b> did Saturday night at Rate Field.</p><p>Usually, they have been sent to the sanctuary of the clubhouse well before that level of carnage has been inflicted. Tough on a pitcher’s ego, and not very helpful to a team’s chances of winning that night.</p><p>Besides Taillon, only one other pitcher this season, <b>Bryan Bello</b> of the Red Sox, had been taken deep five times in a game. Only six <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> pitchers this century have allowed five or more in a start. The last was <b>Matt Swarmer</b>, who somehow surrendered six solo home runs to the Yankees four years ago at Yankee Stadium.</p><p>The White Sox’ barrage Saturday left Taillon in the uncomfortable position of leading the majors in home runs surrendered at 20. That’s in just nine starts spanning only 50⅔ innings, which is not a sustainable rate, especially for a pitcher on a contending team.</p><p>That is not lost on Taillon. He gives up home runs — 20 or more in each of the last seven seasons, including this one. But this is something altogether different. The talk shows and Twitterverse were having a field day at Taillon’s expense.</p><p>“It’s an interesting thing,’’ the 10-year veteran said, “because on the one hand, what I’m doing has worked in the past, and I just had a string of really good starts. So it’s not like I’ve got to rewrite the book or change everything.</p><p>“But home runs are a problem. I just need to find a way to limit those. Taking a bird’s-eye view, is it predictability? I throw six pitches, but to righties I really throw three and to lefties I throw three. So do I just open up the pitch selection and throw everything to everyone all over the place all the time?</p><p>“I mean, I can do it, but we’re just gonna take a look at everything. Throw more fastballs in to lefties, throw more fastballs up, just make them more aware of different areas of the zone because right now I’m not getting away with anything.’’</p><p>Watch any big-league game, Taillon said, and so-called “mistake” pitches don’t all wind up in the seats.</p><p>“They get fouled off or popped up,’’ he said, “but, man, at the end of the day, homers are thrown, not hit.</p><p>“It’s not like I’m out there throwing every pitch down the middle, but unfortunately, with my release and my stuff and how I go about it, I am prone to giving up homers.</p><p>“I just think for me it’s like not to be scared of throwing in the zone, but let’s move their eyes around, let’s throw fastballs in, let’s make them think about the cutter, slider, curve. Let’s make them think about everything.’’</p><h3>Assad to get stretched out</h3><p>The Cubs sent right-hander <b>Javier Assad</b> to Triple-A Iowa with the intention of stretching him out as a starter, manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Sunday. They also selected the contract of left-landed reliever <b>Ty Blach</b> and moved reliever <b>Hunter Harvey</b> to the 60-day injured list to create a roster spot. Blach’s promotion was likely a one-day thing. <b>Caleb Thielbar</b> was at Rate Field and is expected to be activated as soon as Monday for the game against the Brewers.</p><h3>Brewers’ ‘The Miz’ on tap</h3><p>The Cubs are scheduled to face Brewers phenom <b>Jacob Misiorowski</b> on Tuesday. The right-hander averages 99.6 mph on his fastball and threw 10 fastballs 103 mph or faster against the Yankees earlier this month, topping out at 103.6 mph.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" entries.title: First piping plover eggs of the season spotted at Montrose Beach and Waukegan
entries.summary: <p>Two of Montrose Beach's piping plovers, Sea Rocket and Imani, have laid their first egg of the year. </p><p>It’s the third season the beloved birds have nested together at Montrose. The pair is able to lay up to four eggs a season. As of this weekend, one egg was spotted, said Tamima Itani, the lead volunteer coordinator for Chicago Piping Plovers, a volunteer group dedicated to protecting the birds. </p><p>“It’s very exciting that they’re nesting now. We really hope everything goes well and we hope they have chicks,” Itani said.</p><p>It usually takes four to five weeks for a plover egg to hatch, Itani added. </p><p>Imani, the offspring of piping plovers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2024/02/20/chicago-park-district-great-lakes-piping-plover-monty-and-rose-endangered-birds" target="_blank" >Monty and Rose</a>, was hatched at Montrose Beach in 2021. Sea Rocket, who was reared in captivity, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/13/23793029/piping-plover-chicks-released-montrose-beach" target="_blank" >was released at the same beach</a> in July 2023. Since then, the pair has been inseparable.</p><p>Up in Waukegan, plovers Pippin and Blaze have also laid an egg, Itani said. Pippin was a bachelor for the last two seasons at both Montrose Beach and in Waukegan. Pippin <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/04/13/injured-plover-returns-to-montrose-beach-pippin-is-a-trooper" target="_blank" >returned to the area in April</a> with a missing foot and a limp. He otherwise appears to be in good health. </p><p>“We’re really happy for them,” Itani said. </p><p>So far this season in Illinois, about 20 piping plovers have either passed through the state or stopped to breed, Itani said. </p><p>“That’s really mind-blowing,” she said. “That speaks to the success of the recovery efforts for the birds.” </p><p>Piping plovers nearly went extinct in the Great Lakes region. The birds have been on the federal endangered species list for 40 years. But conservation work in Michigan and across the Great Lakes has helped to rebuild the birds’ population. </p><p>For the birds to no longer be considered endangered, there needs to be 150 breeding pairs in the region, 50 of which need to be outside of Michigan, Itani said. Last year, a record 88 nesting pairs were spotted in the area, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.greatlakespipingplover.org/overview" target="_blank" >the Great Lakes Piping Plovers</a>. </p><p>Before the weekend, there were 32 confirmed active nests in the Great Lakes area so far this season, Itani said. That doesn’t include the Chicago and Waukegan nests. </p>

entries.title: Dancers in Chinatown celebrate Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month
entries.summary: <p>Melody Wu, a teacher at the Bridgeport-based DanDance Art Academy, gave her dancers a smiling thumbs-up as they finished a public performance in Chinatown Square.</p><p>The Uyghur ethnic dance, part of an event Sunday celebrating Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month, was the culmination of lots of hard work, Wu said.</p><p>Wu's students have been honored in citywide competitions. And the school’s K-pop group is sending 11 teens to a national competition this fall.</p><p>“The girls are so hardworking," she said. "As a teacher, I’ve been glad to see them improve themselves."</p><p>The showcase featured a variety of dances.</p><p>Performer Zhi Qing Aiu showcased the face-changing art of bian lian. Aiu swapped masks mid-performance, sometimes hidden behind a fan or hand, to show the changing mood of his dance’s story.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> entries.title: Edgar Quero, White Sox rally past Cubs to take crosstown series
entries.summary: <p>Tristan Peters was going to be the White Sox’ hero but the Cubs’ Michael Conforto ripped that away. Finally, the hero ended up being Edgar Quero in the Sox’ 9-8, 10-inning<b> </b>win Sunday, one of the most memorable in the history of the teams’ rivalry.</p><p>After the Cubs had taken an 8-7 lead in the top of the inning, Quero hit a two-run homer off Ryan Rolison, giving the Sox the series win in front of a raucous crowd of 38,608. The Sox finished off a 7-2 homestand, their best of at least nine games since 2008. The Cubs, meanwhile, lost for the sixth time in eight games.</p><p>The Sox, who had been down 3-0 and 4-1, tied the game in the fifth on Miguel Vargas’ two-run double that eluded a leaping Pete Crow-Armstrong in center field. They took their first lead in the eighth on Tristan Peters’ three-run home run off the Cubs’ Phil Maton to take a 7-4 lead.</p><p>Peters, whose homer was his first in the majors, was the preeminent story for about 15 minutes.</p><p>Sox closer Seranthony Dominguez, signed in January to a two-year, $20 million contract, immediately got into trouble by walking Alex Bregman. Vargas then spiked a throw to first on Seiya Suzuki’s grounder to third. That brought up Conforto, whose drive over the wall in straightaway center tied the game and gave the veteran outfielder another clutch hit for the Cubs.</p>
entries.author: Brian Sandalow
